### The Congress that could decide AI [[00:00:00]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=0)

**Rob Wiblin:** We now know the makeup of Congress during what may turn out to be the two most important years for AI that ever occur.

[Democrats won big time](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/2026-midterm-election-results-where-democrats-won/), far more than anyone predicted. They’ll have [at least 250 seats](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/house-results) in the House of Reps, and [56 out of 100 seats](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/senate-results) in the Senate — including seats in Mississippi, South Carolina, and Kansas, a place they [hadn’t won in 100 years](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6028587/adam-hamilton-kansas-senate-political-divides). And they [won Texas](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/texas-results), of all places, by 11 points, sweeping every office in the state.

AI wasn’t a top-three issue in this election, but it was maybe the [fourth or fifth most significant driver](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/exit-poll-trump-midterms-voters-economy-disapproval-rcna607045) of the voter backlash. It’s a place where government policy and what voters say they want are just clearly, massively out of sync.

All of which makes it more likely that Congress takes [major action on AI](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/04/democrats-eye-a-silicon-valley-ai-reckoning-01148624) during this crucial window in its development. So what’s likely to happen, and what are the most likely ways for things to go really well in the next two years?

### Legislating AI will still be difficult [[00:00:49]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=49)

Let’s start with the bad news, at least from my perspective. Despite the massive shift in Congress and the role that AI played in it, passing a strong standalone AI bill still won’t be at all simple.

The first threshold one has to cross to have a shot at passing legislation is to get 60 votes in the Senate to overcome [the filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_in_the_United_States_Senate). That is actually probably possible for an AI bill.

The issue is a lot less partisan in Congress than you might expect, given [Trump’s strong stance](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/03.20.26-National-Policy-Framework-for-Artificial-Intelligence-Legislative-Recommendations.pdf) against [pacing the frontier](https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/) or any binding AI regulation.

Among the general public, Democrats and Republicans feel roughly the same about AI — which is to say, remarkably negative. [Four in five Americans](https://news.gallup.com/poll/694685/americans-prioritize-safety-data-security.aspx) want the government to keep AI safety rules even if it slows down development, including almost 80% of Republicans. And while [67% of Americans](https://yougov.com/en-us/daily-results/20260914-11f9f-1) say they think AI is advancing too quickly, just 2% think that it’s advancing too slowly.

Plus, a number of Republican senators have been leaders in the push to act on AI, including [Josh Hawley](https://cyberscoop.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/09/2026-09-09-Hawley-Letter-to-OpenAI-re-Hugging-Face-AI-Agent-Hack.pdf), [John Kennedy](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5417), and [Marsha Blackburn](https://www.cnn.com/2025/07/01/tech/senate-strikes-ai-regulation-moratorium-agenda-bill), and we can guess that many more are quietly sympathetic.

But the president has a veto over any legislation passed by Congress, and [overcoming that](https://history.house.gov/Institution/Presidential-Vetoes/Presidential-Vetoes/) would require 67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House of Reps. With overall concern at today’s levels, that is going to be pretty hard to achieve — or it would require watering down the rules to the point that they’re not especially useful.

But that is far from the end of the road.

### Four things Congress can do immediately [[00:01:59]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=119)

There are at least four ways Congress can make progress right away, even with a veto hanging over it.

The first is to pass the commonsense measures that are already popular in both parties, some of which might get 70, 80, or even 90 votes in the Senate.

For example, today it seems entirely possible that the Chinese government can and is [stealing model weights](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sella-nevo-securing-ai-model-weights/) from US AI companies — in a sense that actually gives them more extensive access to frontier models than the US government itself has.

Nobody in Congress likes this situation, and legislation could demand that companies [fix it](https://ifp.org/a-sprint-toward-security-level-5/) before they keep going training more powerful models.

There are probably also bipartisan majorities in Congress for [restoring](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/corporations/trump-nvidia-h200-chips-ai-china-rcna248107) and strengthening [export controls to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China), and law enforcement against [chip smuggling](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/california-man-arrested-smuggling-more-300-million-export-controlled-computer-servers-china), which I think would strengthen the US’s negotiating position if it ever does want to push for [an AI treaty with China](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/tom-milton-verification-technology-ai-slowdown/).

It’s less clear, but there are also indications that there might be congressional supermajorities in favour of things like [whistleblower protections for AI staff](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/1792), [mandatory incident reporting to Congress](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/9477), and also so-called ‘[kill switches](https://lieu.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/reps-lieu-and-moran-introduce-bill-require-kill-switch-ai-systems-can)‘.

As the water level rises, the range of provisions that can attract majority support in both parties is only going to keep growing.

Second, there’s must-pass legislation: the bills that keep the government funded, like [the annual defence bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Authorization_Act). These are hard for a president to veto, because it means [a government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_shutdowns_in_the_United_States) or no defence budget. So this is where negotiated deals between parties get done.

The most obvious thing to try to include in such a deal is proper funding to build out [CAISSI](https://www.nist.gov/caissi), the likely home of US AI regulation — something that I’ll come back to later.

The third pathway is the least significant, but I’ll mention it anyway. Cabinet secretaries and many other senior officials need to be [confirmed by the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_consent), so senators can grill nominees for AI-relevant roles, and vote down or hold up anyone whose views on AI are badly out of step with those of the Senate itself.

The fourth pathway is quite big. It’s to hold hearings and collect information. There are so many things that the Senate and the House should demand that company staff answer under oath.

For example: what is the full story of the hack where an AI swarm [took over an OpenAI research cluster](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/)? [We’re still not being told](https://casar.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/casar.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/oversight-letter-to-openai-openai-hugging-face-incident.pdf).

[OpenAI also says](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra/monitorability) it has evidence that using [looped transformers](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/gpt-6-astra-looped-transformers-and) didn’t reduce monitorability much. What are all of the experiments that they conducted to assess that?

Over at Anthropic, what evidence do they have that pushing ahead with more and more [recursive self-improvement](https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai) is [safe or not](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-rd-section-anthropic-risk-report-august-2026-review/)?

What models are OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google training right now, and how much compute are they using?

And have these companies conducted any safety tests with results so embarrassing that they didn’t publish them?

These are all great questions to ask, and probably quite fun for members of Congress as well. Between them, these four pathways could get a lot done over the next two years. But they’re all about working around the veto, not overcoming it.

### Why workarounds won’t be enough [[00:04:25]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=265)

Unfortunately, I don’t think just working around it will be enough to make it through this. We need a much bigger shift in policy than anything I’ve been describing.

At a minimum, we need to [slow down the AI race](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how/) while models are around the human level, to give AI companies breathing room to test the nature and personality of their models, check over the work that they’re doing, and hone their [alignment techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment).

Without that extra breathing room, it seems more likely than not that we produce [superintelligent machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence) that are misaligned but completely [capable of hiding that fact](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking) — and that this, or some other screw-up, leads to total disaster.

[The companies themselves](https://openai.com/index/ai-policy-window/) are [begging to be given this time](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier). But as far as I can tell, we don’t yet have a supermajority in Congress in favour of rules sufficient to accomplish that.

That is a very serious problem, because [more and more evidence](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q35-timelines-update-looks-like-the) is coming out suggesting that it will be possible to fully automate AI R&D [as soon as 2027](https://thezvi.substack.com/p/ai-r-and-d-is-accelerating-towards), and that this will lead to a big speed-up in research progress — including [a new report from METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) that landed last week.

For that reason, we desperately need [California to take big steps immediately](https://secureaiproject.org/california-policy/pacing-the-frontier/) as a stopgap measure until Congress can step in, and I hope to cover that in a separate video.

But the events that did more than anything else to [build support in Congress to act](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/senators-from-both-parties-question-openai-on-breach-of-ai-startup-hugging-face) were [the Hugging Face hacks](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/) and [Jacob Coxon’s resignation](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/09/tech/ai-anthropic-safety).

To change Trump’s perspective, or get a supermajority in Congress to overcome his veto, my guess is that it will take another demonstration of what AI can do, or is willing to do, that’s at least as shocking to people as that was.

### Preparing for future warning shots [[00:05:44]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=344)

[That next warning shot](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-takeover-soon-oversight-monitorability/) could take many different forms.

At the low end, we could have another Hugging Face incident, but one that demonstrates long-term power seeking by the AI, or that interrupts services ordinary people use.

At the high end, we could see [AI cyber capabilities](https://openai.com/index/responding-next-frontier-critical-cyber-capabilities/)[disabling critical infrastructure](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-extinction-explained/), or a rogue AI that [can’t fully be shut down](https://palisaderesearch.org/research/shutdown-resistance), or even [an AI-caused pandemic](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/preventing-catastrophic-pandemics/).

The days and weeks after such an event could well be the most pivotal ones in AI policy — the critical moment that sets us on a better trajectory, or saves us from a much worse disaster later.

Some people should be trying to improve policy today, both for the direct benefit and to build experience and relationships. But if willingness to act can predictably soon be 10 or 100 times greater than it is today, clearly many people should also be preparing for that moment. That means being ready to work 100-hour weeks, and above all, thinking through and drafting excellent legislation now, while there’s still time to think carefully and get it right.

### Why preparation matters [[00:06:35]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=395)

Anyone preparing for that moment should expect a very different political environment from the one we’re in today. I see three main ways that things can predictably change.

Up until now, AI regulation has done everything it can to improve safety while doing as little as possible to interfere with company activities. If a warning shot is severe enough, the public mood may be so furious that that constraint could disappear, or even flip on its head.

Interfering with model training or deployment, or just generally lashing out and interfering with AI companies, may come to be viewed by the public or politicians as actively desirable, rather than something that needs to be minimised.

The second big shift is that the typical legislator in AI regulation discussions is then going to know much less about the topic, so things are going to have much less of a technocratic vibe.

And thirdly, the public is going to be a lot more involved, and politicians will have to sell the steps they’re taking to the general public. That’s going to mean boiling it down to a core simple message, and communicating why what they’re doing is actually going to deal with the problem.

### The slogan will be ‘ban superintelligence’ [[00:07:28]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=448)

My guess is that the simple message more informed groups are going to rally around will be ‘[ban superintelligence](https://superintelligence-statement.org/)‘, or ‘ban superhuman AI’.

It’s a simple idea that’s easy to explain. It makes intuitive sense that it would help. Unlike banning AI entirely, it’s going to seem feasible.

And [polling shows](https://futureoflife.org/recent-news/americans-want-regulation-or-prohibition-of-superhuman-ai/) the US public is already overwhelmingly against the training of superintelligent machines — ones that totally dominate human experts in all domains. It’s a sufficiently natural idea that there’s already [legislation introduced](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5493) in the House and Senate to accomplish that goal: ban superintelligence.

Needless to say, there are massive implementation challenges that people preparing for this moment need to figure out ahead of time. Such as: what’s the best [treaty to immediately propose to China](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15916) to enable both countries to pace the frontier? What specifically are we going to be limiting or banning? And how does the policy shift over time?

One promising answer is that rather than limiting training runs, we require AI companies to spend a [minimum share of their compute](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/how-to-pace-the-us-frontier) serving inference to outside customers. If you set that minimum to 100%, that’s basically a research pause that keeps every AI product running — and it’s actually immediately good for AI users, who will be able to buy inference at much lower prices.

The exit plan would be to gradually tone this constraint down to, say, 70%. But if we get new warning signs, that’s a dial that we can turn back up again to pace the frontier more strictly. Effectively, a regulator could set this number in order to achieve whatever speed of AI progress it thinks is desirable — the same way [the Federal Reserve sets interest rates](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm) in order to keep the economy not too hot and not too cold.

This stuff needs careful forethought and legislative drafting involving technical experts familiar with how the frontier companies work.

### Limit recursive self-improvement [[00:08:58]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=538)

Beyond the big public slogans, there are a few ideas that are too niche to ever be rallying cries, but that I think are worth developing out now, and probably worth including in any emergency response.

The thing I’m most excited by is the idea to [throttle recursive self-improvement](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/how-to-pace-the-us-frontier) using the specific mechanism of prohibiting AI companies from using recent models for their research or any other work.

The rule would be something like: for internal purposes, AI companies can only use models that finished training at least, say, six months ago, and which have already been released publicly.

The companies couldn’t complain that it’s ridiculous and makes their work impossible. Presumably it wasn’t impossible to do their jobs six months ago. And for that reason it wouldn’t by itself stop AI research progress entirely — but it would definitely slow it down, and it would make it much harder for it to ever become truly explosive, or for alignment to go off the rails very abruptly.

That’s because any capabilities gains couldn’t be fed back into the recursive self-improvement cycle for at least six months. We’d also have at least six months for extensive alignment tests of a model before it gets its own hands on the control wheels and is able to design its successor.

The policy also has a more significant slowing effect the stronger and faster recursive self-improvement would otherwise be going, which is exactly the effect we want. If six months turned out to be too little, we could just increase the delay. And if the figure is extended out to one year, or 18 months, or two years, you’re incrementally coming closer and closer to an outright ban on recursive self-improvement.

We ideally don’t want to interfere with research aimed at improving safety and alignment in particular, and to that end, companies could potentially apply to CAISSI for exemptions for particular projects. To give companies less reason to pass off capabilities work as alignment work, the rules could require that any work conducted with the help of more recent models has to be published in full as soon as it’s completed — which would mean that any capabilities research would effectively immediately be shared with competitors.

This approach does have some weaknesses. If a company found an older model was misaligned in some way that they hadn’t appreciated at the time, they wouldn’t just be able to replace it with a new one that they think is more aligned. We’d need to have some workaround to address that.

But overall, this really seems like an idea with legs that’s worth developing in detail. If Congress is willing to take any significant steps to limit AI company research practices in the near future, this is the most valuable rule that I’m aware of to attach to a must-pass bill.

### Enforce monitorability [[00:11:11]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=671)

The next most promising idea, at least to me, is banning scarily high [no-chain-of-thought capabilities](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/eRmzz8J8Qkzqvzrgg/astra-can-do-a-concerning-amount-with-no-chain-of-thought).

In short, you don’t ban models that are too capable, full stop. Rather, you ban models that are able to accomplish too much without writing anything down in their [chain of thought](https://openai.com/index/chain-of-thought-monitoring/) along the way.

If models can’t do very much without a chain of thought, it’ll be a lot easier for us to monitor them, and they’ll have a much harder time [scheming](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/science/stress-testing-deliberative-alignment-for-anti-scheming-training) against users. A rule like that would force companies to go back and figure out how to design AI with a fundamentally safer architecture that has [much less serial depth](https://institute.deepmind.com/essays/the-case-for-reasoning-transparency/).

Another approach people have suggested is banning excessive use of [reinforcement learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning) to generate superpersistent agents, because those [RL environments](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking/) seem to play a very outsized role in [causing AI misbehaviour](https://www.anthropic.com/research/emergent-misalignment-reward-hacking), at least currently. Perhaps you could set a maximum amount of [RLVR-generated data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) that can be used while training models.

Another possibility is that frontier AI training and research should have to be conducted in fully [sandboxed](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/), [air-gapped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_gap_(networking)) facilities.

I don’t know if those ideas can be made to work well in practice. We’re going to need clever technical people to think hard and figure that out.

### Is it useful to stop data centres? [[00:12:12]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=732)

Those more technical ideas are where I’d put my own energy. But alongside ‘ban superintelligence’, I expect the slogan with the broadest support to be something much more concrete: stop building data centres.

Data centres were [directly on the ballot](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/midterm-election-results-data-center-buildout-artificial-intelligence-texas/) in [40-odd places in the midterms](https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/11/06/voters-favored-limiting-data-center-development-in-40-of-41-local-ballot-measures-on-nov-3/), and the anti side won all but one of those elections, often by a ratio of [three to one](https://fortune.com/2026/11/04/ohio-data-center-ballot-measures-midterm-elections/).

And assuming a serious warning shot, preventing more compute coming online is a step in the right direction, for sure. It’s a great place to start building a broader coalition as well.

But if, like me, you’re most worried about [loss of control to AI](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/loss-of-control/), or bio or cyber misuse, or [extreme concentration of power](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/extreme-power-concentration/), it’s probably not the highest-leverage thing to push for individually.

The thing is, if we’re already at the point where loss of control is possible, simply not adding more chips doesn’t make the problem go away. It at best holds it steady.

To lower the risk, you need to restrict company research and deployment practices like I’ve been describing, or you need to start actively disconnecting chips from existing data centres. And you also can’t allow chips to be relocated to data centres outside the US — that’s not much of an improvement. So to be properly effective, a ban on data centre construction would have to be paired with [stronger export controls](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/) as well.

So data centre bans by themselves aren’t top of my list, but they could be one useful part of a broader response package that avoids effectively pouring more fuel on the fire, while we use other policies to help put the fire out.

### The government needs visibility [[00:13:32]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=812)

Whatever mix of bans and limits we end up with, there’s one other piece of the puzzle that would be really easy to underrate, which is making sure the government can actually accurately tell how much danger we’re still in.

If you want to pace the frontier of AI development for years rather than just months, it becomes necessary to progressively add global coordination, and proper enforcement, and [compute controls](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/lennart-heim-compute-governance/) — all of which is possible in principle, but raises the difficulty quite a bit.

To keep escalating like that, it will be necessary for political willingness to act to keep rising in line with the seriousness of the threat. And experience so far shows that simple facts about what AI models can do, and the misaligned things they are doing, and the sloppy company practices that make it all possible — that has done far more to change minds than anything else.

That means it’s incredibly valuable for Congress and the executive to get more transparency into AI companies.

For instance, companies should be required to immediately share any significant accidents or warning signs. CAISSI should automatically get access to any tests or research results conducted by the companies. And really, they should have their own [auditors placed inside the companies](https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/embedded-assessments-for-frontier-ai), keeping tabs on what they’re doing, following [the embedded bank supervisor model](https://www.anthropic.com/news/an-update-on-independent-evaluators).

### We need more AI experts in CAISSI [[00:14:37]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=877)

On top of this, the US government needs its own expert AI body that can make sense of this enormous amount of incoming information, implement regulations that are passed, and adapt them to circumstances over time.

Unfortunately, an organised government agency with top AI experts can’t be thrown together in a few weeks in a crisis, which is why it’s urgent that Congress properly fund the body best placed to play this role, which is the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or [CAISSI](https://www.nist.gov/caissi).

There are great people there, but it’s just way too small and underfunded relative to the scale of the role that we need it to play. It’s getting outclassed — mogged, really — by the equivalent agencies in the UK.

CAISSI runs on [about $15 million a year](https://ifp.org/funding-for-caisi/) with just a few dozen staff, while [the UK’s AI Security Institute](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/about) has over 100 technical staff alone, and about eight times the budget. Britain just committed [another £300 million](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/budget-2026-document/budget-2026-html) to it over the next four years, plus hundreds of millions more for new agencies on AI biosecurity, cyber, and rogue-AI incidents.

Adjusting for its economy, the UK is now spending something like 50 times as much building state capacity in AI. Which is a massive credit to the UK. But it’s also completely nuts.

The effect is that in a serious emergency, the US might be forced to delegate a lot of AI risk assessment to the UK government, because it hasn’t built the capacity to perform core functions for itself. Both parties in Congress and the White House should want to urgently rectify this.

Fortunately, this is exactly the kind of thing that can go into the next government funding bill. Even the White House has asked to [nearly double CAISSI’s budget](https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/cc/06/8b16b75b45afb68086116d28960f/nist-budget-request-fy27.pdf) next year, and I think Congress should go much further.

### Checks and balances [[00:16:06]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=966)

Again, there’s another high-level challenge to deal with here. Almost every step that I’ve described, including a bigger CAISSI — all of it — hands more power to the executive branch. And that power could be used to [strong-arm companies](https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/27/tech/anthropic-pentagon-deadline) into doing things that have nothing to do with safety, if that’s what the executive wants to do.

Ideally, we’d have built-in safeguards against this, such as well-thought-through options for companies to challenge decisions in the federal courts if they’re capricious, or violate [the First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution), or just aren’t credibly justifiable on safety grounds.

And the details are really going to matter here. It’s probably too dangerous to allow companies to get [a preliminary injunction](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/preliminary_injunction) to pre-emptively block rulings from, say, CAISSI. But we do want them to be able to object and overturn clearly political decisions promptly — within two weeks, if at all possible.

In the worst case, if Congress concludes that the executive simply isn’t going to enforce rules that it passes, or it’s only going to use them to pursue partisan political objectives, Congress may be forced to just play an assisting role, helping states like [California](https://www.gov.ca.gov/2025/09/29/governor-newsom-signs-sb-53-advancing-californias-world-leading-artificial-intelligence-industry/) and Texas do the heavy lifting, at least for some period.

The tradeoffs here are pretty difficult to deal with, and they’re another thing that has to be thought through ahead of time, not in the middle of an emergency.

### Don’t stop the states [[00:17:12]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=1032)

Here’s a final trap to watch out for. Until now, the expectation has been that when Congress passes a big set of AI rules, it’s going to [pre-empt the states](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/12/eliminating-state-law-obstruction-of-national-artificial-intelligence-policy/) and [severely limit their ability to regulate AI](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sneha-revanur-ai-advocacy/). By default, though, I think anything like that should be kept out of an emergency bill after a warning shot of some type.

By that point, states may well have [strong rules on the books](https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/governor-hochul-signs-nation-leading-legislation-require-ai-frameworks-ai-frontier-models), and regulatory systems and agencies that have actually been set up and are functioning. And given the goal is to immediately strengthen safeguards, it would be totally perverse to delete those rules, which could have the net effect of at least temporarily loosening controls.

### Have good ideas lying around [[00:17:46]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/congress-ai-policy-after-midterms/?t=1066)

The midterm results substantially increase the chance that Congress will act to reduce AI risk, which is great. But it’s nowhere near guaranteed that this will happen in time, or happen in a really smart way.

If you understand how frontier models actually get trained, this work needs you really badly.

There are people working on these topics at [the AI Futures Project](https://www.aifutures.org/) and [Secure AI Project](https://secureaiproject.org/), among many others. And some politicians who have [deep familiarity with these issues](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/nathan-calvin-sb-1047-california-ai-safety-bill/) — most notably [Scott Wiener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Wiener) — are going to be joining Congress for the first time soon, and they’ll no doubt be looking to develop proposals.

It’s a cliché that when a crisis finally comes, what gets done depends on “the ideas that are lying around.” But it’s a cliché because it’s mostly true.

Political will on this topic is only going to go in one direction. Our job is to make sure that when the moment comes, the ideas lying around are good ones — ideas that will actually fix the problem. That’s something people listening to this show are [unusually well placed to help with](https://80000hours.org/ai/).

If we pull it off, these might just be the two years during which an AI catastrophe is averted.

And on that note, I’ll speak with you again soon.

title: Have your AI call my AI
content:
Sharp lawyers have often used the fine print to win an advantage in a contract. It’s called the fine print for a reason–you’re not supposed to read it. But you should.

Now, armed with AI, it’s significantly easier to bury arcane, unfair or unanticipated clauses in agreements, even (and especially) if we don’t expect it.

You shouldn’t sign anything until you’ve had your AI read it. And if it’s important, have your lawyer and her AI read it too.

The next step seems reasonable to me: You and I describe our agreement in plain English and then our mutual AI’s work out a written agreement that actually captures what we’ve agreed on. And for the avoidance of doubt, append each AI’s interpretation to the contract itself.

It shouldn’t be confrontational or adversarial. After all, it’s an _agreement_.

title: Giant, Fruit-Eating Bats Are Shrinking
content:
On Madagascar, a furry creature with a puppy-like nose is a key player in pollination. The bat, called the Madagascan flying fox (_Pteropus rufus_), gulps down fruits, flowers, and nectar, resulting in dustings of pollen all over its face. With a wingspan of up to 5 feet, these bats travel as far as 30 miles during their foraging journeys, unwittingly spreading pollen far and wide.

But a [new study](https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/advance-article-abstract/doi/10.1093/jmammal/gyag092/9002374) published in the _Journal of Mammalogy_ shows that Madagascan flying foxes are physically shrinking over time. Biologists who had conducted fieldwork in Madagascar noticed that the flying foxes they observed appeared to be smaller than the ones housed in the mammal collections at the Field Museum in Chicago.

**Read more: “**[**Mother Bats’ Hearts Quicken When They Hear Baby’s Cries**](https://nautil.us/mother-bats-hearts-quicken-when-they-hear-babys-cries-1286069)**”**

“I was thinking about a million different angles to explain why the bats were getting smaller. I wondered if it was related to changes in temperature or habitat,” said lead author Emily Cornelius Rohs, a postdoc at the Field Museum.

Her coauthor Steven M. Goodman, however, had a different hypothesis: commercial hunting. These flying foxes are hunted for meat and are classified by the Malagasy government as a game species. Their population was tallied at about 300,000 in the early 2000s, but continued commercial exploitation has reduced it by about two-thirds.

To see whether the perceived change in body size correlated with the onset of large-scale hunting, Ruhs and Goodman reviewed the Madagascar flying fox collections at nine museums in the U.S. and Europe. They measured the skulls and teeth (the body parts most often preserved) of 121 specimens collected over roughly the last 150 years. Next, they compared pre-hunting and post-hunting sizes.

The results showed a drop in size beginning in about 1980. “If you’re the biggest bat in the sky, you might be the easiest target. You’re also going to provide a hunter with the most meat,” explained Ruhs.

While other factors could contribute to the trend—such as deforestation and climate change—hunting warrants targeted attention because flying fox meat provides a fair share of the protein for local diets, now showing up on roadside restaurant menus (“hotely”) and even supermarkets.

This, of course, is no good for the flying fox—both in terms of its size and its overall survival. And, since smaller bats constitute smaller ferries for pollen, it also shrinks the role of Madagascan flying foxes in pollination. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: A Chemical Fingerprint in Ancient Rocks Suggests Plate Tectonics Began 2.5 Billion Years Ago
content:
[Plate tectonics](https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/plate-tectonics/) is one of the reasons Earth looks so different from its planetary neighbors.

The movement of enormous chunks of our planet’s crust builds mountain ranges, triggers earthquakes, shapes our oceans and continents, and helps regulate Earth’s climate and magnetic field over deep time.

This process may also be key to sustaining the kind of long-term habitability that allowed complex life to evolve. But exactly when it began has been a long-standing mystery.

In [new research](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2026.0587), we studied chemical fingerprints in more than 1,000 rocks to look for clues – and found clear evidence for when this remarkable shift occurred.

**Why Plate Tectonics Matter**

Many scientists believe plate tectonics provides the long-term stability that [keeps our planet life-friendly](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaw4326), unlike tectonically “dead” worlds such as Venus and Mars.

But [debate has raged](https://www.jstor.org/stable/26601825) over when this process began: has it run throughout Earth’s entire 4.5-billion-year history, or did it “switch on” at some point along the way?

For much of its early history, Earth may have been [mostly covered by oceans](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/planet-earth-through-the-ages/), without the shifting, colliding plates that build tall mountains – which in turn erode away, supplying the nutrients to feed marine life.

The question is hard to settle because plate tectonics are very good at destroying the evidence. Where plates collide, some old crust is dragged back down into the mantle, and the crust that is thrust upward to form mountains also starts eroding away, which erases the geological record.

Often, all that survives are chemical fingerprints preserved in ancient rocks that have endured for billions of years, against the odds.

**Reading the Fingerprints in Rocks**

In our new study, we studied one such fingerprint.

New continental crust – the ground we stand on – doesn’t always form fresh from crystallising mantle magma. Often it’s made from melting older rock that was already sitting inside existing crust.

That process leaves a lasting chemical trace in the new rocks, a bit like the DNA a child inherits from their parents. This is the fingerprint we studied.

In some minerals (feldspar and some sulfide minerals, in our case) this fingerprint can survive largely undisturbed for billions of years.

We analyzed over 1,200 rocks, some newly analyzed by us, others compiled from earlier studies, from ancient landmasses across Australia, Africa, North America and Europe, spanning nearly four billion years of Earth’s history.

Some of the many samples analyzed for this study. The mineral crystals inside retain their chemical fingerprint largely unchanged for millions to billions of years. _Credit: J. Liebmann_

**The Vanishing Signal**

We found a striking pattern in the fingerprints. Rocks older than about 2.5 billion years carried the unmistakable signature of very ancient crust, which appears to have formed about four billion years ago.

In geological terms, this is not too long after Earth itself formed. This ancient crust material was melted and remelted repeatedly, for well over a billion years, to produce the granite-like rocks that made up much of Earth’s earliest continents.

Then, around 2.5 billion years ago, that fingerprint vanishes abruptly. We searched through hundreds of younger rocks without ever finding the distinctive signature of those ancient crustal reservoirs again.

A granite dome in Ghana, photographed during fieldwork. _Credit: J. Liebmann_

**A Turning Point for Earth**

We think the vanishing of this fingerprint marks a fundamental reorganization in how Earth builds continents. Before 2.5 billion years ago, our results suggest the same ancient continental material was melted over and over again, with little input from other sources.

Then things shifted. Instead of melting ancient rocks to form new crust, the planet started producing crust from a mix of old and new sources. This is something we still see happening today at the edge of tectonic plates, where volcanoes bring fresh molten rock up from the mantle while older crust is also being recycled.

As a result, the fingerprint of the ancient crust disappeared. So we believe this shift 2.5 billion years ago was when plate tectonics may have begun.

There is other evidence of major changes around the same time, too. There were more changes in rock chemistry and alterations in the thickness and composition of the crust, and Earth’s first supercontinent also formed in this era.

Taken together, all this evidence shows there was a turning point in how our planet works at this time. And as a result, Earth’s surface developed the environment life needed to flourish.

We still don’t know exactly what triggered the start of plate tectonics, but we’re continuing to chase an answer. For now, our results offer another piece of the puzzle of when Earth’s unique tectonic engine kicked into gear. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The World’s Largest Marine Turtle Makes a Move South
content:
Leatherbacks aren’t only spectacular for bodies that rival grand pianos in size and weight, but also for their [temperature tolerances](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0013925). By taking refuge in cool upwellings, they can inhabit tropical waters up to 86**°**F; on the flip side, by warming their bodies with activity and insulating fat, they can tolerate waters as cold as 32°F. But even leatherbacks have their limits.

A [recent study](https://ccb.kglmeridian.com/view/journals/ccab/aop/article-10.2744-CCB-1686.1/article-10.2744-CCB-1686.1.xml) in the journal _Chelonian Conservation and Biology_ found that warming oceans are shifting the nesting sites of leatherback sea turtles (_Dermochelys coriacea_)to cooler waters. Typically, the critically endangered population of eastern Pacific leatherbacks concentrates its nesting along the west coasts of Mexico and Costa Rica. Now, though, they’re showing up about 1,000 miles south in Ecuador.

**Read more: “**[**How Sea Turtles Find Their Way**](https://nautil.us/how-sea-turtles-find-their-way-238070)**”**

“Historically, observing female Eastern Pacific leatherbacks on Ecuador’s beaches was a rare or unusual event, but our findings suggest they are adapting their reproductive cycle to thrive and survive in coastal Ecuador,” explained lead study author Juan José Alava, a biologist at Simon Fraser University in Canada.

Alava and coauthors in Ecuador compiled records of leatherback nesting activity along Ecuador’s coast from as far back as 1980. Their compilation included peer-reviewed studies as well as conservation reports, government survey records, and validated social media sightings. They also tracked the El Niño and El Niña events that sway sea surface temperatures.

They found record-breaking numbers of nesting females, with the uptick starting around the year 2000. Hatchling leatherback turtles hadn’t been reported along Ecuador’s coast since 1983. So, the emergence of nests in the winters of 2020 and 2021 in Manabí Province was a cause for celebration. And both 2025 and 2026 saw additional hatching success of nests that were relocated to protected areas.

“It signals new hope for a subspecies of leatherback on track for extinction in the eastern Pacific within 60 years,” added Alava.

Unfortunately, though, a higher frequency of leatherback strandings has also been observed of late. From 2011 to 2026, at least 35 dead leatherbacks were confirmed to have beached on the Ecuadorian coast. Many of those strandings were associated with injuries from fisheries and other human activities.

And so, Pacific leatherbacks haven’t quite found safe harbor yet. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Why Sleep Might Not be as Restorative as We Get Older
content:
Every night, you get [brainwashed](https://nautil.us/how-sleep-cleans-the-brain-1279438).

As you’re sleeping, slow brain waves trigger gentle pulses of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that bathe your brain, flushing out the waste that’s accumulated during the day. It’s an important process, and one that’s been linked to cognitive health, neuroprotection, and memory consolidation. Of course, as we age, we also tend to sleep less. Now, a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s43587-026-01270-4) in _Nature Aging_ is taking a look at what happens to these revitalizing waves as we get older.

A team of neuroscientists led by imaging specialists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology recruited some young (ages 18-39) and older (ages 60-84) volunteers to spend a night getting their brains scanned. While they dozed, the participants had their noggins imaged by both fMRI and a modified MRI technique to measure CSF flow. Their brain activity was also recorded by an EEG machine. As the younger group drifted off, their slow EEG waves intensified—and the CSF pulses followed suit. Among the older participants, however, these CSF waves were markedly weaker.

**Read more: “**[**Is Sleeping in on the Weekends Bad for Your Heart?**](https://nautil.us/is-sleeping-in-on-the-weekends-bad-for-your-heart-1286260)**”**

To find out what was behind the differences, the researchers observed their brain activity while they were awake. First they tested their neurovascular coupling, or the relationship between brain activity and blood flow, by using an image of a flickering checkerboard. This usually cranks up neural activity which in turn increases blood flow. It did, for both groups, but the older cohort again showed an attenuated response.

The same pattern showed up in tests of the brain’s vascular system. The researchers asked the participants to hold their breath in order to trigger a carbon dioxide build-up to dilate the brain's blood vessels. On average, older participants showed a weaker vasodilation.

Still, the attenuated neurovascular coupling and decreased blood flow didn’t account for the full gap between the young and old. In other words, there’s more to this story. “Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it’s really hard to disentangle the individual factors,” study author Sydney Bailes of MIT explained in a [statement](https://news.mit.edu/2026/waste-clearing-waves-in-brain-during-sleep-are-impaired-in-older-adults-1113). “We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual’s CSF flow might be more or less impaired.”

Importantly, not all of the older participants experienced a drop-off in CSF pulses. Some of them were indistinguishable from their younger counterparts. “It’s really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults,” senior author Laura Lewis of MIT said. “We are really interested in what’s different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.”

While we wait for someone to find out, remember to get a good night’s sleep—weak waves or not. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Public Health Initiatives Looked Like in the Middle Ages
content:
Medieval Europe isn’t exactly known for its major advances in public health, but a new [book](https://www.scup.com/doi/full/10.18261/9788294167104-26-06) is challenging those assumptions. In it, the authors take a multidisciplinary approach to better understand how the citizens of Trondheim, an ancient Norwegian city, grappled with growing concerns about illnesses.

Trondheim’s population exploded in the Early Middle Ages, increasing from roughly 250 around 950 CE to 1,500 by the 12th century, then doubling during the High Middle Ages to about 3,000. It was during this period that monks and other scholars arrived, including the archbishop. With them, they brought new theories of disease spread, notably the miasma theory that illnesses were spread by foul odors.

**Read more: “**[**The Medieval Friar Who Foretold Carl Sagan’s “Star-Stuff”**](https://nautil.us/the-medieval-friar-who-foretold-carl-sagans-star-stuff-1248330)**”**

And Trondheim had plenty of foul odors.

Dirt from pits of human waste were actually used to level the town for expansion. To mask the nasty smells, the people of Trondheim relied on fresh wood chips leftover from construction—at least for a time. According to [study](https://www.scup.com/doi/full/10.18261/9788294167104-26-06) author Elisabeth Forrestad Swensen of Trondheim’s Museum of Defence History Rustkammeret, this potpourri practice stopped in the mid-13th century as trees grew scarce (possibly because of global climate shifts caused by the eruption of an Indonesian volcano in 1257). With the miasma theory taking hold and the offensive stench returning, something had to be done.

Curiously, Swensen’s analysis of Trondheim’s ancient infrastructure revealed that the number of latrine pits actually _dropped_ during the population explosion and subsequent wood-chip shortage. So where did the waste go? According to Swensen, it was carried out of town… to the farmland where Trondheim grew its food. The result was a population riddled with parasites.

“An analysis of the contents of these latrines reveals that nearly the entire population was infected with roundworms,” Swensen explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1151600). “Latrine waste was incorporated into manure once it began being transported out of the city center. Roundworms thrive especially well in manure. This manure was spread across the city’s agricultural land where food was grown, allowing the roundworm parasite to enter the food supply, and consequently, the people living in the city.”

Importantly, this isn’t another story about how backwards people were in the Dark Ages. Instead, it’s a lesson about how Medieval populations collectively approached very real public health issues. The waste removal was well-intentioned, and according to prevailing theories of the time, successful too.

“The medical understanding of the period makes it likely that no one saw the connection between the removal of latrine waste and the high degree of parasitic infections in the population,” Swensen wrote. “This well-thought-out plan to ensure the health of the people by treating latrine waste so carefully backfired due to the lack of knowledge about parasites and hygiene.”

They just failed to learn that age-old lesson: Never shit where you eat. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: When Envy is a Virtue
content:
Our oldest stories teach us that envy is an emotion to be feared. It can lead to moral bankruptcy, violence, the collapse of friendships, families, and kingdoms. It is the cause of the first murder on Earth described in the Bible and the Quran: Cain kills his brother Abel because he is favored by God, and is then filled with grief and guilt, cursed to wander the land forever restless and alone. Across the middle east, South Asia, and the Mediterranean, a tradition of believing that envious glances can bring tragedy leads some to wear amulets to ward off the so-called evil eye.

Envy made the list of seven deadly sins for a reason.

**Read more:**[**“Are Some People Addicted to Revenge?”**](https://nautil.us/are-some-people-addicted-to-revenge-1238041)

But envy can also contain clues about how to orient our lives, argues social scientist Stacy Kim, if we can listen to what it is telling us. The independent researcher and life coach is author of the new [book](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/stacy-s-kim-ph-d/envy/9781538776711/?lens=balance), _Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want._ Kim says converting envy into drive is not an easy process, but the English language does not help because we lack the vocabulary for it.

I spoke with Kim about the differences between malicious envy and benign envy, Snow White, the Buddhist concept of Muditā, or sympathetic joy, Korean economics, and what to do if you think someone might envy you.

**Envy as a source of torment and ruin is a theme in some of our oldest stories across religious and cultural traditions. Why do you think that is?**

First, we don’t like to feel behind or lacking. It just makes us uncomfortable. At the same time, we’re social beings, so most people don’t like feeling bad about somebody else. On top of wanting something somebody else has, now I’m also feeling like a bad person. So it’s a confluence of lots of different negative emotions.

Then we have culture or religion on top of that. I looked into the deadly sins and cardinal sins and found that, over time, they’ve become more of a condemnation or judgment, but it didn’t start out that way. [They were originally [compiled](https://digitalcommons.csbsju.edu/sot_pubs/56/) as more of a physician’s checklist, symptoms of a troubled soul that warranted attention rather than eternal damnation.] So that adds guilt and shame. I think that’s a problem.

Another problem is that we’re linguistically challenged in English. In Korean, there’s another word for envy, but also German, Dutch, Russian. There’s a second word for envy that aligns with the research around benign versus malicious envy. English speakers don’t have that extra way to describe our squishy feelings. We also mix it up with jealousy, which is actually something else.

**What is the difference between envy and jealousy?**

Envy is simply wanting something that someone else has. It’s a negative experience that we feel. Jealousy is more of a fear of a loss of an important relationship to a rival, which means there’s three parties involved—I am jealous when my husband looks at another woman. It can also happen in a work situation: I am jealous when my boss starts paying attention to the new hire and thinks the new hire is so great. Maybe I used to be the star, and so I’m losing that relationship with my boss.

In my book, I talk about how as a kid, I was very jealous that my brother got so much attention from my parents when it came to things like achievement and career. They really invested in his career in ways that they didn’t invest in mine, and I felt very jealous about that. I was also envious that my brother had the attention that I did not, so both things were going on with me.

**Interesting. And what are the differences between malicious and benign envy?**

Malicious envy is when you’re more preoccupied with the person who has the thing that you want, and you don’t want that person to have it. Benign envy is more focused on what you want. Let’s say I’m the evil queen and I want the beauty that Snow White has. Benign envy would be where the queen goes, “Oh, let me figure out from Snow White what she uses for her skincare. How does she keep her face so young and beautiful?” Instead, the queen says, “I need to kill Snow White so that I can be fairest of them all.” That’s malicious envy. But it also makes for a better story. You look at all these great movies or stories and benign envy would be boring. It would be inspirational, but it would be boring. I think that’s part of what is going on, too.

In Korean, there are a few words for benign envy: _bureowoyo_ or _seonmang_. And you usually, you can tell a person, “Ah, Kristen, ‘bureowoyo,’” and it translates as, “I envy you. I wish I could be like you. I admire you.” It’s all rolled into one. And because you’re able to express it, it’s a conversation starter.

I think that people usually respond in Korea by saying, “Oh, you can do this, too! This Is what I did.” Korea is a very collectivist society, so they will say, “Oh no, I didn’t do this alone. I did it thanks to my teammates, thanks to my boss, thanks to my parents,” attributing success to the group. I think that’s why culture really matters.

**You argue that envy can be used to benefit oneself. How does this work?**

First, you acknowledge, “Oh, I’m feeling this way. I’m human.” Then when you can, you take a look at that envy and try to decipher what it’s really trying to tell you. I use the acronym SIREN to go through the four components of envy.

S is for “similar target.” Envy usually occurs when we’re close to the person or similar to the person that has something we want. A young cellist isn’t going to envy Yo-Yo Ma, she’s going to admire him. The young cellist is going to envy the first chair, especially if they’re second chair. What’s really fascinating is that there are researchers who have found that admiration is not as motivating as benign envy. It lights that fire in you.

I stands for “intangible desire,” and I think it’s the most important piece of this. It’s usually not really the thing that you think you want. It’s the feeling that you think that thing will bring you. And if you look at that, there’s often more avenues to get that feeling. My clients come to me and say, “Oh, I didn’t get that promotion that I wanted. I lost it to some other guy. I need to find another job.” I’m like, “Well, wait a minute. Let’s just first figure out what did that promotion mean to you? What was it that you wanted? And is there another way to get that?” Don’t trash all the career equity you built up with your organization. Maybe first look at what it is that you want. It could be more financial security. It could be a recognition for a job well done. It could be the opportunity to mentor other people. What is that intangible desire?

R is “relevant comparison.” Let’s go back to that cellist. That cellist is not going to be envious of their friend who’s a tennis player, because tennis doesn’t mean anything to them. I was just in LA where cars are a huge part of daily existence, but I don’t care about cars. I live in New York City. I take the subway, bus and Uber if I need to. But if I see a writer get a clip in a magazine that I wish I could have gotten into, oh my gosh, I’m going to feel so much envy. In my book, I describe how for a long time I denied myself that. I was envying other writers, but I wasn’t paying attention to my envy. I was doing other things. I didn’t devote time to developing my craft because I was ignoring my envy. That’s why I think for so many people, it’s really good to pay attention. What domain am I envying? And maybe that’s something that I need to explore.

The last thing is N, “negative emotion.” It gives you a gauge. The more negativity you feel, the more we have to pay attention to it. I’ll envy stuff I see on Instagram. Like, I’ll see, “Ooh, I like that sweater.” But when I close my phone, I forget about it. But if I see a writer who gets a clip somewhere, and it sticks with me the next day or the next week, I know that it’s something that I need to pay attention to.

**Once you figure out what it is you actually desire, what do you do about it?**

For a long time, I envied Gretchen Rubin. I thought, “Wow, she’s writing all these really cool things, but I’m not going to read her book because I just don’t want to deal with it. I don’t like the feelings that I’m getting. For a long time, I didn’t read her books, and how ridiculous, because once I started reading her books, I was thinking, “Oh my gosh, she’s brilliant. She’s actually way far ahead of me. I can’t be comparing myself to her. I need to do the work.”

It’s not that I want to beat Gretchen Rubin, I want to be like her. In order to be like her, I need to figure out how she did what she did. She was doing the exact kind of work that I wanted to be able to do. I was just ignoring all of that and going about trying to build my coaching practice. Then I realized, wait a minute, this is something that I want, this is a career avenue, this could help my coaching practice. I was limiting myself because I was so focused on trying to suppress my envy instead of look at it.

**Do you think there are any gender differences in terms of how people experience envy?**

There’s some research around that, but I found it to be not helpful. I think that everyone envies. It’s a universal thing. If you don’t envy, it means that you’re not striving. You’re not trying to improve yourself. You’re not trying to succeed in a group. You’re not being competitive. People who are competitive, people who are striving, people who are ambitious, are naturally going to feel envy.

**Can envy be used to the benefit of groups?**

Yes. I use Korea as an example, because they couldn’t go after their former oppressor, the Japanese, but the Korean government definitely used envy to motivate Korean citizens to do well. I was born in Korea, brought to the United States as a baby, and then I moved back when I was about 10.

I was cultured in the U.S. and knew things about freedom, equality, things like that. And I go to Korea and I’m like, “Oh my gosh, I’m stuck at the bottom. Nobody cares about girls.” It’s a poor country. And when I go to school, first of all, the boys are favored, but also everybody’s being told we gotta study hard because we have to beat Japan. This was in the ‘70s, and once a week, I would hear a teacher say, “Gotta study hard so we can beat Japan.”

It was really in the culture. If you think about Korean economics, back in the ‘70s, it wasn’t the beautiful country that you see on K-dramas now. It was really struggling. We only got hot water in the mornings and nights. Electricity was so expensive. It took us a year to get a landline phone when we first moved back. Everyone was striving, and everyone wanted to collectively bring the country up out of being considered a third world country into a more modernized first world country that could compete with Japan. That’s what they did. They went after the car industry, electronics, and then later after K-Pop. Koreans don’t have natural resources, but we have lots of people, so we could go into entertainment. All of those industries were heavily subsidized by the government.

**Envy is a part of the story of Buddhism. The Buddha’s cousin is envious of him and tries to have him killed and then suffers for that later. But Buddhism also has a name for a cure, which is****_Muditā_, and translates as sympathetic joy, taking real delight in the fortune of others. I wonder if that is a step on the way to using envy for motivation or if it sits in opposition to it.**

What I’ve noticed over time is that just saying, “Oh, let’s be grateful,” or, “Let’s have joy for other people,” is wonderful advice, but you can’t get there without first acknowledging your envy and examining your envy. It’s just unrealistic to jump from, “Oh, I don’t have what I want, but then let me be grateful for the things that I do have.” It doesn’t address the envy. A better approach is to recognize that envy is a negative emotion, and it’s something that’s trying to tell us something important.

Anger, fear, guilt, grief, all of these negative emotions are trying to remind us, “Hey, there’s something important you need to pay attention to.” Fear means that there’s danger. Anger means that maybe there’s an injustice. Envy shows us what we want. Grief shows us that we’ve lost somebody that we love, and we need to remember them or honor them. If we just bury these negative emotions, they’re going to seep out in ways that are not going to be helpful to us. We also need a little bit of stress to motivate ourselves. I’m not talking about chronic depression or chronic envy. I’m talking about just listening to smaller doses of negative emotion when they occur.

**What do you do if you think you’re the object of someone else’s envy?**

First of all, I think that you can never tell. There’s no facial expression for envy. You might be able to sense it from a combination of other cues. But trying to judge whether somebody is feeling envy is not that helpful, because only they know.

Envy can be directed to three things that can give you a good life. First, meaningful work. What kind of work would you do even if people didn’t pay you? For some people it’s organizing spreadsheets. For other people, it’s interviewing people. Envy can help you discover what that is.

Number two is meaningful relationships. Sometimes your envy points you to relationships that you want to cultivate and deepen.

And third is, how can you make a contribution? How can you serve others? If you’re sensing envy from someone, one thing you can do is to think, “Okay, well, how can I serve this person? How can I help this person? Or how can I deepen my relationship with this person?” That is far more useful and gratifying in the end than trying to compete with this person or put this person down or try to prove that person wrong. Using warmth, collaborating, connecting, is more interesting and useful. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Some Antidepressants May Work Better Than Others Long Term
content:
[Anew review](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(26)00326-3) has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in _The Lancet Psychiatry_, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the _best_ antidepressants?

**Why Do People Take Antidepressants Long Term?**

Around [one in seven Australians](https://www.beyondblue.org.au/mental-health/depression) will experience depression during their lifetime.

[Treatment can involve](https://www.blackdoginstitute.org.au/resources-support/depression/treatment/) psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, [3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant](https://www.aihw.gov.au/mental-health/topic-areas/community-based-services/mental-health-prescriptions#Prescriptions-by-medication-type).

For adults with depression, [clinical guidelines](https://www.ccm.health.qld.gov.au/management-of-diagnosed-conditions/depression#section__4medicinesfordepression2679) recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, [it may be appropriate to reduce](https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/stopping-antidepressants-when-and-how.html), and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. [One 2022 study](https://doi.org/10.1192/bjo.2022.522) found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

[Another Australian study](https://doi.org/10.1002/pds.70267) found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

**What Did the Researchers Find?**

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomised controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

**How Reliable Are the Findings?**

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all [PBS-dispensed prescriptions](https://www.pbs.gov.au/statistics/expenditure-prescriptions/2024-2025/Expenditure-prescriptions-report-tables-2024-25.PDF) in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

**What This Research Can’t Tell Us**

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience [withdrawal symptoms](https://www1.racgp.org.au/ajgp/2026/june/continuing-antidepressants-or-not) when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

**What’s the Best Fit for You?**

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
